title: Precision bounds for characterising quantum measurements

paper_content.abstract: Quantum measurements, alongside quantum states and processes, form a cornerstone of quantum information processing. However, unlike states and processes, their efficient characterisation remains relatively unexplored. We resolve this asymmetry by introducing a comprehensive framework for efficient detector estimation that reveals the fundamental limits to extractable parameter information and errors arising in detector analysis-the detector quantum Fisher information. Our development eliminates the need to optimise for the best probe state, while highlighting aspects of detector analysis that fundamentally differ from quantum state estimation. Through proofs, examples and experimental validation, we demonstrate the relevance and robustness of our proposal for current quantum detector technologies. By formalising a dual perspective to state estimation, our framework completes and connects the triad of efficient state, process, and detector tomography, advancing quantum information theory with broader implications for emerging technologies reliant on precisely calibrated measurements.
paper_content.introduction:
Measurements hold a special place in quantum mechanics, bridging quantum states and real-world classical observations. This probabilistic transition from the quantum to the classical, originally postulated by the Born rule1, typically washes out key quantum features like superposition and entanglement, thereby limiting the information that can be extracted from a quantum system2. The modern theory of quantum measurements has evolved well beyond the observe-and-collapse paradigm3–5, encompassing generalised measurements such as weak measurements that blur the line between observation and interaction5–9. Experimental practice has lent further credence to the utility of these generalised measurements5,8–10, for instance, by showing the advantage of entangling measurements for the precise characterisation of quantum states11–15.

The measurement of a quantum state constitutes one part of the triad of quantum states, processes and detectors that forms the basis of any quantum information protocol16. From quantum estimation theory, the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) provides a metric for the distinguishability of parametrised quantum states and processes, leading to bounds on estimation errors known as quantum Cramér-Rao bounds (CRBs)17,18. Strikingly, despite the fundamental and practical importance of quantum detectors, whether similar bounds exist for general quantum detectors remains an open question. In this paper, we answer this question. More precisely, we ask whether information-theoretic precision bounds exist for the accurate estimation of detector parameters.

The aforementioned disparity is particularly surprising given the dual nature of states and measurements in quantum theory2—a symmetry suggesting their informational properties should be balanced. However, while provably optimal state estimation protocols are known, existing approaches to detector estimation often overlook the efficiency of the process19,20, and thus fail to inform optimal estimation strategies. Optimal detector estimation strategies are essential to extract maximal benefit from future quantum devices. For example, precise characterisations of state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors on quantum computing platforms hinge on reliable detector reconstructions21. Large uncertainties in reconstructed detectors propagate into SPAM error estimates22 that could limit platform performance and impede effective error mitigation. Similarly, photonic experiments rely on photodetectors23–27 whose precise calibration must be known a priori. Although coherent state probes are one option for photodetector tomography16,24,25, it remains unclear to what extent quantum properties of light such as entanglement and squeezing, could improve this precision28. These questions underscore the need for a general framework for efficient and high-precision reconstruction of the measurement operators.

In this work, we formulate and prove the maximum information extractable from probing unknown quantum measurements and call it the detector quantum Fisher information (DQFI). The DQFI leads to fundamental limits, that is, the quantum Cramér-Rao bounds (QCRBs), on the uncertainties in locally estimating parameters of measurement operators19,20,29–32, thereby setting a performance benchmark for past and future detector tomography experiments. In addition to providing the first fundamental bound for detector estimation, the DQFI enables us to draw the following physical insights: 1) We draw a direct analogy between the DQFI and the well-known state quantum Fisher information (SQFI), finding some similarities and some surprising differences. 2) We apply the DQFI to noisy on-off single-photon detectors16,24,25 and implement the first provably-optimal detector estimation experiment using the IBM platform. 3) We show that the proposed DQFI framework provides an alternative approach for optimal sensing of a quantum process18, which requires both optimal probe states and optimal measurements (Fig. 1(c)). In practice, our alternative approach could lead to more appropriate benchmarks in settings where probe preparation capabilities by far exceed control over the measurement device.

Overall, our work reveals surprising connections between the theories of state and detector tomography while highlighting the unique aspects of detector analysis. These findings complete the triad of optimal state, process, and detector tomography (Fig. 1)16,24, paving the way for a more balanced role of states and measurements in precision quantum metrology.
paper_content.results:
Introduction to the framework
Before introducing precision bounds for the estimation of quantum measurements, we briefly recap the concept of efficiency and how it leads to precision bounds in quantum state estimation17,29–34. The task here (Fig. 1(a)) is to estimate parameters θ of an unknown state ρ θ, by first measuring the state via a m-outcome POVM, Π ≡ {π 1,…,π m}, and then processing the measured probabilities, p θ (j)=Tr(ρ θ π j ), to get the parameter estimates17. The efficiency or effectiveness of the measurement Π in extracting parameter information depends on how sensitive its measured statistics are to changes in the parameter value. In the local setting, where the unknown parameters are close to some known true values17,30, efficiency is quantified by the classical Fisher information (CFI) of the distribution17,35–37,

F θ [ρ θ,Π] := ∑ j∈[m] (∂ θ p θ (j))2 / p θ (j) = E p θ (∂ θ log p θ )2 , (1)

capturing the variance of the parameter-derivative ∂ θ p θ/p θ of the distribution (abbreviating ∂ θ := ∂/∂ θ and [m]:={1,…,m}). The minimum mean-squared error (MSE) of parameter estimates achievable (on average per trial) using a measurement Π is given by 1/F θ, as per the classical CRB (CCRB)31. Accordingly, optimal measurements are those that maximise the CFI in Eq. (1), thus minimising the CCRB and yielding the most precise estimates17,38,39. However, maximising this non-linear quantity is challenging in practice, even more so in the multi-parameter case38,39, so the state QFI (SQFI) I θ of state ρ θ was introduced as an upper bound to the maximum CFI over all measurements29–31. The SQFI is defined as

I θ [ρ θ]:=Tr(ρ θ L2 θ )=E ρ θ [L2 θ ], and satisfies

max Π F θ [ρ θ,Π] ≤ I θ [ρ θ] (2)

for any valid ρ θ, with equality holding in several cases17,34. The symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) operator L θ appearing in the definition generalises the classical logarithmic derivative ∂ θ log p θ in Eq. (1) implicitly via L θ ρ θ+ρ θ L θ=2∂ θ ρ θ. Following Eq. (2), the QCRB given by 1/I θ lower-bounds the MSE of estimates for any measurement Π, thus setting a precision bound31. In the following, we introduce a general framework for bounding estimation precision for parameters of quantum measurements. To start off, we consider detector models with a single unknown parameter; these are relevant for practical single-photon detectors and noisy qubit detectors. Then, we generalise the framework to multi-parameter scenarios, addressing general quantum detector tomography.

Single-parameter detector estimation
The task here (Fig. 1(b)) is to characterise an unknown m-outcome measurement Π θ ≡ {π jθ } j∈[m] by first probing it with a known quantum state ρ in, and then processing the measured probabilities, p θ (j)=Tr(ρ in π jθ ), to obtain parameter estimates. The efficiency of the probe state ρ in in extracting parameter information from Π θ is determined by the CFI, F θ [ρ in , Π θ], which leads to the CCRB, 1/F θ, lower-bounding MSE when using this probe. Thus, the optimal or most precise probe state, ρopt, is the one maximising the CFI, i.e.,

ρopt[Π θ] := argmax ρ in F θ [ρ in , Π θ], (3)

F θmax [Π θ] := max ρ in F θ [ρ in , Π θ].

The maximisation in Eq. (3) has no known analytical solution, though numerical techniques from channel literature may be applicable40. Specifically, by translating the detector POVM to Kraus operators for quantum-classical maps (particular choice of Kraus set shown in Eq. (27)), the maximisation for F θmax can, in principle, be converted to a maximisation over all equivalent Kraus operators through a numerical semi-definite program40. In practice, however, this approach is computationally demanding due to the large number of Kraus operators for a measurement channel. The question of the optimal probe state is thus a significant hurdle for detector tomography, although it has been addressed for specific measurement channels41,42. The lack of efficiently computable precision bounds for the minimum MSE, 1/F θmax , for detector estimation reveals a gap in our understanding of the information content of measurements and resulting fundamental limits on estimation errors.

We now clarify how the domain of maximisation in Eq. (3) corresponds to various probing strategies for detector estimation. Let H d denote the d-dimensional Hilbert space of probe states and D(H d ) the space of density matrices on H d. The simplest probing strategy is to pick a single state, ρ in , from D(H d ) to probe the detector, repeatedly and independently. Alternatively, one may use an ensemble of p different probe states, ρ k ∈ D(H d ) for k=1,…,p, each with probability q k (∑ k q k=1). Which strategy is ultimately favoured? As we show in Lemma 1 in Methods, from the convexity of the CFI37, a single quantum state is sufficient to be optimal.

Central to the CFI and the SQFI is the logarithmic derivative quantity: both information measures capture the variance of this quantity, as in Eq. (1). To quantify it, we introduce the SLD operators for each measurement operator. For each outcome j ∈ [m] of Π θ, we define an SLD operator L jθ via

L jθ π jθ +π jθ L jθ := 2∂ θ π jθ : (4)

This implicit definition has known solutions in terms of the measurement operators and their parameter derivatives (Eqs. (18), (19) in Methods)43. More importantly, the SLD operators let us express the measurement probabilities p θ (j|ρ)=Tr(ρπ jθ ) and their derivatives ∂ θ p θ (j|ρ)=Tr(ρ∂ θ π jθ )=Re Tr(π jθ ρL jθ ) as linear operations on the state and the measurement (where Re[⋅] denotes real part)17,34. These two expressions, when substituted into the CFI in Eq. (1), open the door to operator inequalities that can gauge F θmax without actual optimisation17.

DQFI definition
To upper-bound F θ by an expression independent of ρ, we borrow from state estimation a chain of inequalities17,34 that, when applied to the CFI expressed in terms of π jθ , L jθ , and ρ, yields

F θ [ρ, Π θ] ≤ ∑ j∈[m] |Tr(√π jθ ρ L jθ )|2 / Tr(ρπ jθ ) ≤ Tr(Q θ ρ), (5)

where Q θ := ∑ j∈[m] L jθ π jθ L jθ is a positive semi-definite operator. The first inequality above relies on Re[z]2 ≤ |z|2 for complex number z, whereas the second is the operator Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. In state estimation we obtain the measurement-independent SQFI I θ at this point, but here the trace quantity upper-bounding F θ still depends on ρ. Our final step settles this by maximising both sides of Eq. (5) over the probe space D(H d ), resulting in F θmax ≤ max ρ∈D(H d) Tr(Q θ ρ)= ||Q θ ||2 sp , where ||⋅||2 sp denotes the largest eigenvalue (or spectral radius) of Q θ. Moreover, the probe state maximising Tr(Q θ ρ) is the eigenvector of Q θ corresponding to its largest eigenvalue—this state is thus always pure.

These results lay the ground for defining the DQFI: an upper bound to the maximum CFI that leads to precision bounds for detector estimation. We propose two definitions for the DQFI.

Definition 1. (Spectral DQFI). Define the spectral DQFI J jj,θ of a measurement Π θ ≡ {π jθ } j∈[m] as

J jj,θ [Π θ] := || ∑ j∈[m] L jθ π jθ L jθ ||2 sp , (6)

where ||X||2 sp denotes the spectral radius or largest eigenvalue of operator X.

A simpler but less tight upper bound on F θmax worth consideration is Tr Q θ. In fact, Tr Q θ= ∑ j∈[m] Tr(π jθ L j 2 θ ) resembles the SQFI I θ. Assembling the measurement operators and their SLD counterparts into md × md block-diagonal operators Π θ,bd := ⊕ j∈[m] π jθ and L θ,bd := ⊕ j∈[m] L jθ reveals Tr Q θ=Tr(Π θ,bd L2 θ,bd )=I θ (Π θ,bd ). This approach is justified in that Π θ,bd is trace-constant (though not unit-trace) like a state and L θ,bd is indeed its SLD operator when treated as such. This weaker upper bound results from treating the measurement as an unnormalised, higher-dimensional state.

Definition 2. (Trace DQFI). Define the trace DQFI J Tr,θ of a measurement Π θ ≡ {π jθ } j∈[m] as

J Tr,θ [Π θ]:= ∑ j∈[m] Tr(L jθ π jθ L jθ ). (7)

Having proposed two definitions for the DQFI, we must compare the two to understand their maximum disagreement and cases where they are equivalent. It is evident from the positivity of Q θ that J jj,θ ≤ J Tr,θ. On the other hand, the largest eigenvalue of Q θ cannot be smaller than the average of its eigenvalues, so that J Tr,θ ≤ d J jj,θ. This leads to the following ordering of the DQFIs,

1/d J Tr,θ ≤ J jj,θ ≤ J Tr,θ ≤ d J jj,θ : (8)

The cause of the disagreement clarifies why the spectral DQFI is tighter—it respects that quantum states are normalised, so that probing along multiple directions requires sacrificing some probability of detection, and hence parameter information, along each direction. Nonetheless, the trace DQFI serves as a simpler upper bound that is more amenable to analytical evaluation.

To consolidate the two DQFI definitions, we propose Theorem 1 in the following.

Theorem 1. (DQFI upper-bounds maximum CFI). For estimating quantum detectors, the spectral DQFI J jj,θ and the trace DQFI J Tr,θ upper-bound the maximum CFI over probe states, F θmax , as F θmax ≤ J jj,θ ≤ J Tr,θ.

Proof. The proof follows from Eqs. (5) and (8) and is provided in Methods.

Theorem 1 leads to the trace QCRB 1/J Tr,θ and the spectral QCRB 1/J jj,θ, which lower-bound the minimum MSE of estimates as 1/J Tr,θ ≤ 1/J jj,θ ≤ 1/F θmax , thereby setting precision bounds for detector estimation.

Example 1. We now present a simple example to illustrate the importance of the DQFI. Consider a qubit Z-basis detector with inherent bit-flip noise4 of unknown strength p (0 ≤ p ≤ 1), corresponding to the POVM Π p ≡ {π 1p ,π 2p } with

π 1p = (1-p 0; 0 p), π 2p = (p 0; 0 1-p). (9)

Figure 2(a) illustrates the Fisher information in estimating p for both non-optimal and optimal probe states. We find that the spectral DQFI (dashed black curve) is tight, as it equals the maximum CFI F θmax . The Fisher information for probe states notated as |θ,ϕ⟩ := cos(θ/2)|0⟩+exp(iϕ)sin(θ/2)|1⟩ is depicted as circular markers (orange, purple and blue) on dashed lines for non-optimal probes, and as star-shaped markers (golden) for the optimal probes. The DQFI J jj,p is 4/(1/〈Z〉2-(1-2p)2) where 〈Z〉=Tr(ρZ) is the Pauli Z expectation of ρ. The CFI is maximised at 〈Z〉=±1, corresponding to |0⟩ or |1⟩, attaining a maximum of F pmax =1/p(1-p) in either case (golden points). As Q p=1/p(1-p) 1 2, its eigenstates are also |0⟩ and |1⟩. Thus, the maximum CFI over probe states equals J jj,p and is attained by probes |0⟩ or |1⟩, in agreement with J jj,p. Here we have J Tr,p=2F pmax =2J jj,p, displaying the maximum disagreement possible for d=2.

Attainability of DQFI
In the above example, the spectral DQFI is attainable, i.e., J jj,θ=F θmax , and the optimal probe states are among the basis states. These two statements are generally true for diagonal or phase-insensitive measurements, because inequality (5) is saturated, as we state in the following theorem.

Theorem 2. (Attainability for diagonal measurements). For estimating a phase-insensitive detector represented by a diagonal POVM Π θ, the DQFI J jj,θ is attainable, i.e., J jj,θ = F θmax , and an optimal probe exists within the family of basis states.

Proof. The proof is presented in Supplementary Mat. I.

Phase-insensitive measurements feature prominently in detector characterisation experiments, in part because they do not require phase stabilisation of probes16,24. Indeed, avalanche photodiodes (APDs)16,24, multiplexed photon-number-resolving detectors16,24,25, and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors26,27,44 have been experimentally characterised in this setting. Given the extensive usage of these detectors across quantum technologies, understanding the information-theoretic bounds for estimating them has practical implications for benchmarking existing approaches to detector characterisation and designing more effective strategies. Our result in Theorem 2 means that the spectral QCRB sets the ultimate precision limit here.

The proof of Theorem 2 also covers measurements that are simultaneously diagonalisable independent of the parameters (see Supplementary Mat. I). This category includes qubit detectors with phase-flip noise (Fig. 2(b)) and bit-phase-flip noise (Fig. 2(c))4, so the spectral DQFI is tight for all single-Pauli error qubit detectors. More generally, we find a necessary condition for attainability of the spectral DQFI to be that the SLD operators commute, [L jθ , L kθ ]=0, akin to compatible multi-parameter state estimation14,17,36,45,46 (see Theorem 3 in Methods for the complete set of necessary and sufficient attainability criteria). However, if the SLD operators do not commute, the spectral DQFI could be unattainable even in the single-parameter regime, which is not the case in state estimation. Interestingly, in this case, the attainable bound can be computed through a semi-definite program (Supplementary Mat. II) that effectively incorporates non-Hermitian components into the SLD operator definition in Eq. (4) (see Methods).

Platform demonstration
We now consider a simple, but practically relevant and experimentally feasible example, of estimating a qubit detector affected by dephasing noise4. Given that dephasing is particularly prominent on current quantum computing platforms47,48, its precise characterisation is crucial for effective noise control and suppression. Other noise models4 are deferred to Supplementary Mat. III.

Example 2. Consider a generic dephased qubit projective measurement, corresponding to the POVM Π p ≡ {π 1p ,π 2p } with elements

π 1p = 1/2 (1 + (1-2p)cosθ sinθ e-iϕ; (1-2p)sinθ eiϕ 1-cosθ), π 2p = 1/2 (1 - (1-2p)cosθ sinθ e-iϕ; -(1-2p)sinθ eiϕ 1+cosθ), (10)

where p denotes the unknown dephasing strength (0 ≤ p ≤ 1/2). Here, the noiseless measurement Π ideal corresponding to p=0 is assumed known. It corresponds to projections along polar and azimuthal angles θ and ϕ on the Bloch sphere (double arrows in Fig. 3(b)), via two orthogonal projectors, |± θ,ϕ⟩, given by the nontrivial eigenvectors of π 1p |p=0. The spectral and trace DQFI can be calculated as

J k,p = sin2θ / p(1-p) & J Tr,p = 2sin2θ / p(1-p) : (11)

The two optimal probe states, ρ± opt, are both pure and have phase ϕ, thus lying in the same vertical plane as measurement projectors |± θ,ϕ⟩, as shown in Fig. 3(a). This observation, magnified in Fig. 3(b), provides an intuitive explanation of the optimal probes (black dots in Fig. 3(b)): they are the pure states that align perfectly with the measurement direction upon dephasing. The polar angles θ ± opt of these optimal probes, given by tanθ ± opt = ±tanθ/(1-2p), can be deduced geometrically from Fig. 3(b).

We now experimentally implement Example 2 on an IBM Eagle r3 quantum computer as follows. First, we introduce dephasing noise of fixed strength p=0.2 by interacting the probe qubit with an ancilla qubit (Fig. 3(c)). Then we estimate the noise strength using a range of probe states, including both optimal and non-optimal ones (see Methods for details). Critically, the noiseless measurement is fixed at (θ, ϕ) = (π/8, 0), differentiating the problem from state or process estimation. In Fig. 3(d), we compare the experimental MSEs for each probe state (blue dots) to the CCRB 1/F p (black curve) that gives the theoretical minimum MSE20 for this probe state and to the MSEs from noiseless simulation (green dots). The spectral QCRB 1/J k,p (horizontal blue dashed line) lower-bounds the MSE for any probe state. The theory-optimal (vertical black dashed line), simulated-optimal and experimentally-inferred optimal probes agree within confidence intervals (green and blue regions), consistent with platform noise.

In contrast to previous efforts to characterise the platform’s SPAM errors through detector tomography22, which do not use optimal quantum states, our work provides the first instance of provably optimal detector tomography.

Multi-parameter detector tomography
In quantum state estimation, there are many physically motivated scenarios where we will want to estimate multiple parameters simultaneously13,14,49–54. Similarly, the example is full detector tomography, where the maximal number of unknown parameters is simultaneously inferred (see below and Refs. 16, 24 for more examples). For state estimation, it is known that measuring the parameters simultaneously can provide greater sensitivity compared to measuring them sequentially55. Analogously, multiple parameters of a detector can be successively estimated using the single-parameter framework56, but achieving the ultimate precision limit requires the simultaneous estimation of all parameters. In this setting, the CFI is a matrix reflecting the probe’s sensitivity to each parameter individually as well as correlations in sensitivities to multiple parameters (defined in Eq. (SM.VII.1), Supplementary Mat. VII). The corresponding QCRBs minimise a weighted-sum of the different parameter variances and covariances18, but an ensemble of probe states is generally required (see discussion in Methods). For simplicity, here, we set the weight to identity and minimise total MSE of the parameters, though our techniques also apply to arbitrary weight matrices (see Supplementary Mat. VII). Below, we propose two QCRBs that lower-bound the attainable minimum total MSE, which is defined as the minimum CCRB over all probing ensembles,

CCCRB := min Tr(F θ -1) : (12)

We first extend the trace DQFI to the multi-parameter setting. For estimating n real parameters, θ:=(θ 1,…,θ n), the trace DQFI from Def. 2 symmetrically extends to the n×n real matrix J Tr,θ with elements

(J Tr,θ ) jk := 1/2 ∑ l∈[m] Tr(L l θ j π l L l θ k +L l θ k π l L l θ j ), (13)

where L l θ j is the SLD operator for the lth outcome and the jth parameter. This matrix upper-bounds the CFI matrix for any probing strategy as J Tr,θ ≽ F θ (Theorem 5 in Supplementary Mat. VII), where A ≽ 0 denotes A is positive semi-definite. The trace QCRB, CQCRB Tr := Tr J Tr,θ -1, thus lower-bounds CCCRB in Eq. (12). However, due to the limitation discussed below Eq. (8), the trace QCRB is generally unattainable, as in Example 3.

Next we consider the more complex problem of extending the spectral DQFI to the spectral QCRB, denoted CQCRB k. This is done through an efficient semi-definite program (in Supplementary Mat. VII), where we define a linear objective that is maximised, symmetrically extending Tr(Q θ ρ) from Eq. (5) to multiple parameters. This results in a bound tighter than the trace QCRB, see Supplementary Mat. VII for details. Notably, the spectral QCRB does not require considering an ensemble of probes, unlike the minimisation in Eq. (12), thus offering a practical computational advantage.

Example 3 below compares the two QCRBs to CCCRB, showing the spectral bound to be tight for an experimentally relevant problem16,24,25.

Example 3. Consider the tomography of a phase-insensitive, on-off qubit detector. The POVM Π θ ≡ {π 1θ ,π 2θ } representing such a measurement may be parametrised as

π 1θ = (θ/2 0; 0 1-θ/2), π 2θ = (1-θ/2 0; 0 θ/2). (14)

The trace DQFI for simultaneously estimating θ≡{θ 1,θ 2} is

J Tr,θ = diag(θ 1(1-θ 1), θ 2(1-θ 2)),

and the resulting QCRB is CQCRB Tr = ∑ j=1 2 1/θ j(1-θ j). The spectral QCRB for this problem is

CQCRB k = (∑ j=1 2 1/√(θ j(1-θ j)))2 = Tr J Tr,θ -1 = CQCRB Tr + 2/θ(1-θ)θ 2(1-θ 2).

The spectral QCRB is attainable, i.e., CCCRB=CQCRB k. The optimal probing strategy requires an ensemble of two states: |0⟩ and |1⟩ prepared with probability q and 1-q in the proportion q/(1-q) = √(θ 1(1-θ 1))/√(θ 2(1-θ 2)).

Probeincompatibility effect
An interesting feature of Example 3 is that the optimal multi-parameter probing strategy is a convex mixture of the single-parameter optimal probes, namely, |0⟩ and |1⟩ for θ 1 and θ 2, respectively. Although this may not hold for generic multi-parameter models, it underscores the fact that when the optimal single-parameter probes for different parameters are incompatible, termed probe incompatibility in Ref. 56, there is an uncertainty trade-off in simultaneous multi-parameter estimation. Naturally, we can expect the optimal simultaneous strategy to generally outperform the optimal strategy that utilizes a fraction of detector uses to estimate each parameter separately. This latter strategy, which we call sequential multi-parameter estimation, is connected to the total QFI metric56, and we compare our bounds to this metric in Supplementary Mat. VIII. While the comparison shows the spectral technique to produce a tighter bound than the total QFI metric56, the former approach may still be viewed as a special case of a particular choice of channel purification and computation of the corresponding QFI matrix.

Application to photodetector tomography
Example 3 generalises to phase-insensitive measurements of higher-dimensional states, such as the APDs experimentally tomographed in Refs. 16, 24, 25. These detectors correspond to diagonal two-outcome measurements in the photon number basis for the continuous-variable state space, truncated at some large dimension d. The spectral QCRB here, CQCRB k = (∑ j=1 d 1/√(θ j(1-θ j)))2, is tight and sets the precision limit for APD tomography. Attaining this precision requires preparing an ensemble of photon-number states {|j⟩}, each with probability q j ∝ √(θ j(1-θ j)), and assigning a higher q j to states |j⟩ that produce more uniformly distributed detection probabilities. Interestingly, the spectral QCRB in Eq. (15) mirrors the Gill-Massar QCRB for state estimation57, with similar behaviour seen in Fig. 2(d) for the simultaneous estimation of bit-flip and phase-flip rates (Example 4 in Supplementary Mat. VII).
paper_content.methods:
Probing strategies for detector estimation
Local unbiased estimation. In the local estimation setting, where unknown parameters θ are close to known true values θ*, the Fisher information framework requires locally-unbiased estimators, meaning estimators with zero bias at the true parameter values17,35,70. Effectively, this constrains how the probabilistic detector outcomes are mapped to corresponding predicted values for the unknown parameters20. In linear estimation20,28, this is done through a classical estimator function represented by an m×n real matrix Ξ jk that, given a detector outcome j∈[m], predicts the estimate Ξ jk for θ k(k∈[n]). The overall estimate produced for each θ k is then ∑ j p θ (j)Ξ jk. The local-unbiasedness condition is then ∑ j p θ (j)Ξ jk |θ=θ*=θ k. The maximum-likelihood estimator is asymptotically unbiased, and therefore can saturate the CCRB in that limit20.

Single-parameter detector estimation. We first present Lemma 1, establishing single-probe strategies to be sufficient for optimal single-parameter detector estimation.

Lemma 1. For single-parameter detector estimation, a single-probe strategy is optimal and at least one optimal state ρopt ∈ D(H d ) exists that attains F θmax in Eq. (3).

Proof of Lemma 1. Suppose, to estimate a single parameter θ of a measurement Π θ, we probe with two distinct states, ρ 1 ≠ ρ 2, ρ 1, ρ 2 ∈ D(H d ), with probabilities q 1 and q 2 = 1-q 1. The joint list of probabilities,

plist={q 1 p θ (1|ρ 1), ..., q 1 p θ (m|ρ 1), q 2 p θ (1|ρ 2), ..., q 2 p θ (m|ρ 2)},

forms a valid distribution and, as q j are (by definition) independent of θ, we see from Eq. (1) that the CFI of plist,

F θ [plist]=q 1 F θ [ρ 1, Π θ]+(1-q 1)F θ [ρ 2, Π θ], (16)

is a convex combination of the CFIs of each probe ρ k individually. Unless the two individual CFIs are equal, the combined CFI F θ [plist] is smaller than the maximum individual CFI. Even if the two individual CFIs are equal, combining them with the only probe ρ 1 or only ρ 2 is sufficient for proving optimality. Thus, for single-parameter detector estimation, a one-state probing strategy is optimal.

Lemma 1 says that for single parameters, the maximisation in Eq. (3) can be performed over ρ in ∈ D(H d ).

Multi-parameter detector estimation. For multi-parameter problems, Lemma 1 does not hold and an ensemble of probes is generally required for optimality. This is because multiple unknown parameters cannot be uniquely determined without sufficiently many linearly-independent outcome probabilities. The multi-parameter CFI matrix F θ for an ensemble {q k, ρ k} k∈[p] comprising p probe states is a convex sum of the individual CFI matrices F θ [ρ k, Π θ] = ∑ k q k F θ [ρ k, Π θ], (17)

similar to Eq. (16). Here, the difference from the single-parameter setting is that the CCRB Tr(F θ -1) requires matrix inversion of F θ. We note that even if the individual CFI matrices are equal, the combined CFI matrix F θ [ρ k, Π θ] = F θ [ρ k, Π θ] is not necessarily equal to the individual matrices, and the inverse of the sum is not the sum of the inverses. In general, the minimum number of probes required for estimating n parameters is ⌈n/(m-1)⌉, where m is the number of outcomes. For n parameters, the optimal strategy is an ensemble of probes {q k, ρ k} k∈[p] that can be used to estimate each parameter simultaneously. However, this minimum number of probes merely guarantees the feasibility of multi-parameter estimation, whereas optimality may require even larger ensembles.

Notably, an ensemble of p different d-dimensional probe states can be realised through access to an ancillary system, A, that can be measured perfectly. This involves preparing a single bipartite-entangled state in D(H d ⊗ HA p ), where HA p denotes the p-dimensional Hilbert space corresponding to system A. For example, the ensemble {q k, ρ k} can be realised by preparing the state ∑ k √q k |ρ k⟩ ⊗ |k⟩A and measuring the ancilla perfectly in the {|k⟩A} basis28. In this sense, Lemma 1 extends to multi-parameter problems, with the optimisation domain becoming ρ in ∈ D(H d ⊗ HA p ).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper introduces new tools to determine the ultimate precision limits of quantum detectors. Detector characterization involves determining the associated POVMs, a task addressed by quantum detector tomography (QDT). In QDT, an unknown element \Pi_k is characterized through a set of known measurements using known input probe states. By performing many repetitions on multiple copies of each probe state, one can estimate \Pi_k, thereby allowing the inverse problem to be solved.
Following the pioneering work of Ian Walmsley's group, QDT has been performed for a wide range of detectors, including SPADs, time-multiplexed detectors, transition-edge sensors, superconducting nanowire detectors, and even the human eye. Due to the complexity of the task, various advanced methods have been developed, such as the Fitting of Data Patterns, self-guided tomography, compressed sensing tomography, and techniques based on neural networks. To the best of my knowledge, all of these approaches rely on fidelity (or variants thereof) for benchmarking.
The current work introduces a novel tool: the detector quantum Fisher information (DQFI). The concept is elegant and the theoretical development is clear. The authors propose two definitions of DQFI—one tighter than the other. While this is insightful, I would appreciate a clearer operational preference or justification for using one over the other.
The authors draw an analogy with the standard quantum Fisher information (QFI). But we know that for pure states, QFI reduces to the variance of the generator. In this sense, QFI provides a lower bound on the mean square error (MSE), which can be related to fidelity. From a benchmarking standpoint, I question whether this represents a significant advance over existing approaches in QDT.
More importantly, it is well known that a key requirement for QDT is that the set of probe states must be experimentally feasible. This means the states must be well-characterized themselves. In standard tomography once the QFI is known and the quantum Cramér-Rao bound (QCRB) is shown to be saturable, one can advantageously identify the optimal probe states for characterization. The authors focus on the single-parameter case, where the situation is relatively simple. Can this be done for QDT?
However, a complete QDT requires a multiparameter scenario, where the QCRB is generally not saturable. In standard QDT, the set of reference states must be tomographically complete; i.e., they must span the space of POVMs to enable inversion. In photodetector measurements, this is relatively straightforward. Coherent states of an optical beam serve as ideal candidates: they are overcomplete and can form a tomographically complete set by varying amplitude (e.g., via attenuation with a beam splitter) and phase (e.g., with a delay line). Crucially, such states are easy to generate using lasers.
A question that remains is whether the proposed DQFI can be used to identify optimal probe states for full QDT. In the standard multiparameter QFI framework, one can convert the QCRB matrix into a scalar bound (e.g., via a trace with a weighting matrix) and thereby derive optimal states. Would a similar approach be possible or meaningful in the DQFI context?
In summary, this is a well-written and rigorous work introducing new concepts that may prove important in refining the limits of QDT. I recommend it for publication. However, I believe that addressing the concerns mentioned above would enhance the readability and practical impact of the paper.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors investigate the precision achievable in estimation of parameters of general quantum measurements. The authors introduce detector quantum Fisher information, investigate its properties and present applications of the established formalism. The present study is comprehensive and it nicely complements the earlier results established of optimal estimation of parameters encoded in quantum states. As pointed out by the authors in the Supplemental material, there are close connections between quantum measurements and quantum processes. The quantum measurement can be seen as a specific instance of a quantum process (or quantum channel), where the output state is one of orthogonal states associated with the measurement outcomes, c.f. Eq. (SM8.3) when traced over the second degree of freedom. Nevertheless, the quantum measurements play so important role that it is fully justified to treat them separately and establish a theory which provides bounds on precision of estimation of parameters encoded in the measurements. Given the central role that sophisticated quantum measurements play in modern quantum technologies and quantum computing architectures the potential impact and importance of the present work are high enough to in principle deserve publication in Nature Communications.
There are several points that should be considered by the authors before the manuscript could be published:
1) In the Supplemental Material 7 the authors consider a scenario where two copies of the measurement are available. In this case, entangled probe states may be optimal and may provide advantage. What about using entangled probes when probing a single copy of the measurement. Suppose a pure bipartite entangled states of systems A and B is prepared and the measurement is applied to system A. Subsequently, also system B is measured and the measurement on B can depend on the outcome of the measurement performed on system A. Could such scenario provide any advantage with respect to using only a single system A to probe the characterized quantum measurement? Note that the entanglement of A and B need not be maximal.
2) The authors base their work on the widely utilized concept of Fisher information. To saturate the Cramer-Rao bound, an unbiased estimator is usually required. The authors should clarify in more details which estimators do they have in mind in general, whether they assume the maximum likelihood estimator in the asymptotic limit of very large number of samples.
3) In the Supplemental Material 3, the authors provide an example of a linear estimator of parameter p, Eq. (SM.3.2). What are the signs of the coefficients alpha and beta in this estimator? It seems that one of the coefficients is negative. In principle, the estimator can yield a negative value of the estimated parameter, which would be unphysical. This may happen in case of low number of samples and if the true p is close to 0. While such situations may be rare in occurrence, the authors should comment on this, because e.g. changing the negative p to p=0 could introduce a bias in the estimator.
4) The authors should check Eq. (SM.8.16).
5) In Figure 1 in the Supplemental Material, symbol theta denotes both the angle of a probe quantum state and also the unknown parameter to be estimated. The authors should check the notation used in this figure.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors of the paper, propose the concept of detector quantum fisher information (DQFI), which in their words, feels the gap in the triad “State, Process and Measurements”. They claim that while State and Process estimation are well investigated fields, the Measurement estimation problem is not. They derive the upper bound on the achievable classical information in terms of DQFI, which they show to be saturable for a subclass of diagonal povms. They propose also a generalization to multi-parameter case, and discuss an experimental using the IBM quantum computing platform.
The paper is in my opinion correct, and also highlights in an interesting way the relevance of measurement estimation problem. There is a serious issue with the paper, however, which authors are either not aware or intentionally avoid discussion of.
Any quantum measurement is a special case of a quantum channel, more concretely a quantum-classical channel! Given any generalized measurement, with measurement operators \pi_j, I can construct a corresponding channel with Kraus operators K_j = |j> \sqrt{\pi_j}, where outputs represent measurement outcomes.
I can now use all the results from quantum channel estimation theory to obtain channel QFI – which in this case will correspond to DQFI. In particular, in J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. , 41 p. 255304 (2008) , it is shown that channel QFI is upper bounded by 4 | \sum_i \dot{K}_i^\dagger \dot{K}_i|, where the norm is the spectral norm, and \dot{K}_i are derivatives of Kraus operators. In our case since, we can plug in operators K_j = |j> \sqrt{\pi_j}, and use identity \dot{(K_i^\dagger K_i)} = \dot{K_i}^\dagger K_i + K_i^\dagger \dot{K_i}. to effectively get the result (6) obtained by the authors.
Moreover, the above result from quantum channel estimation theory is much stronger than the result presented by the authors, as one can prove its general saturability provided one minimizes the channel over different Kraus representations. Furthermore, this problem may be implemented as a simple SDP programme as was shown in Nat. Commun. , Vol. 3 p. 1063 (2012). Hence, these tools are much more powerful than the ones proposed by the authors.
Regarding the multi-parameter case, it should be stressed here, that the non-trivial issue here is the ‘probe-incomplatibilty’ , which has been also investigated thoroughly in the quantum channel estimation literature, see e.g. Phys. Rev. X , Vol. 12 p. 011039 (2022). In particular in this reference, a generalization of Fujiwara bound to multiparameter case is given. I presume that this bound again would allow for a more efficient numerical analysis than the bound proposed by the authors, as it again may be solved using the SPD. This at least should at least be tested and compared.
In the light of these results, the novely of the presented work is not as high as might seem at a first sight. Still, despite this harsh criticism, I would not formulae here a negative recommendation yet. Provided the Authors are able to show that they are able to propose an improved tools compared to the ones I mentioned above, making use of the particular structure of the quantum-claasical channel that represents the measurement process and showing that they are superior to the all-purpose channel estimation methods.
In particular, if authors were able to show that minimization over different Kraus representations, that is required to find the channel QFI in the general case, can be simplified for the detector QFI case – ideally solved analytically!- and show some insight behind it I would regard this as an important contribution to the field. In the same spirit If the authors show that their multi-parameter approach is superior to existing channel estimation approaches, this would be an argument in favour of this paper to be published in Nat Comm. Otherwise, the paper may at most be regarded as a nice highlight of an important special case of a problem which has a known solution, and as such does not meet the standards of Nat. Comm.
Apart from this main criticism, I have some minor remarks:
- Above Eq.(2) the authors write: “. However, this maximisation is not tractable in general [38, 39],” This is only true for multi-parameter case. For single parameter this problem is completely solved, and hence this sentence will be misleading for the readers, as immediately below the authors present single parameter formulas
- Authors do not mention the possibility of using an ancilla with which the probe state is entangled. I guess in this case this would not help, as the quantum channel we consider is quantum-classical, but It would be nice at least to comment this.
- Below Eq.3 Authors write “The maximization is not analytically tractable”. This is true, but in the light of what I wrote, above it is also slightly misleading, as there are efficient methods to find channel QFI with a simple SDP programme.

## Abstract

Quantum measurements, alongside quantum states and processes, form a cornerstone of quantum information processing. However, unlike states and processes, their efficient characterisation remains relatively unexplored. We resolve this asymmetry by introducing a comprehensive framework for efficient detector estimation that reveals the fundamental limits to extractable parameter information and errors arising in detector analysis-the detector quantum Fisher information. Our development eliminates the need to optimise for the best probe state, while highlighting aspects of detector analysis that fundamentally differ from quantum state estimation. Through proofs, examples and experimental validation, we demonstrate the relevance and robustness of our proposal for current quantum detector technologies. By formalising a dual perspective to state estimation, our framework completes and connects the triad of efficient state, process, and detector tomography, advancing quantum information theory with broader implications for emerging technologies reliant on precisely calibrated measurements.

## Introduction

Measurements hold a special place in quantum mechanics, bridging quantum states and real-world classical observations. This probabilistic transition from the quantum to the classical, originally postulated by the Born rule1, typically washes out key quantum features like superposition and entanglement, thereby limiting the information that can be extracted from a quantum system2. The modern theory of quantum measurements has evolved well beyond the observe-and-collapse paradigm3–5, encompassing generalised measurements such as weak measurements that blur the line between observation and interaction5–9. Experimental practice has lent further credence to the utility of these generalised measurements5,8–10, for instance, by showing the advantage of entangling measurements for the precise characterisation of quantum states11–15.

The measurement of a quantum state constitutes one part of the triad of quantum states, processes and detectors that forms the basis of any quantum information protocol16. From quantum estimation theory, the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) provides a metric for the distinguishability of parametrised quantum states and processes, leading to bounds on estimation errors known as quantum Cramér-Rao bounds (CRBs)17,18. Strikingly, despite the fundamental and practical importance of quantum detectors, whether similar bounds exist for general quantum detectors remains an open question. In this paper, we answer this question. More precisely, we ask whether information-theoretic precision bounds exist for the accurate estimation of detector parameters.

The aforementioned disparity is particularly surprising given the dual nature of states and measurements in quantum theory2—a symmetry suggesting their informational properties should be balanced. However, while provably optimal state estimation protocols are known, existing approaches to detector estimation often overlook the efficiency of the process19,20, and thus fail to inform optimal estimation strategies. Optimal detector estimation strategies are essential to extract maximal benefit from future quantum devices. For example, precise characterisations of state preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors on quantum computing platforms hinge on reliable detector reconstructions21. Large uncertainties in reconstructed detectors propagate into SPAM error estimates22 that could limit platform performance and impede effective error mitigation. Similarly, photonic experiments rely on photodetectors23–27 whose precise calibration must be known a priori. Although coherent state probes are one option for photodetector tomography16,24,25, it remains unclear to what extent quantum properties of light such as entanglement and squeezing, could improve this precision28. These questions underscore the need for a general framework for efficient and high-precision reconstruction of the measurement operators.

In this work, we formulate and prove the maximum information extractable from probing unknown quantum measurements and call it the detector quantum Fisher information (DQFI). The DQFI leads to fundamental limits, that is, the quantum Cramér-Rao bounds (QCRBs), on the uncertainties in locally estimating parameters of measurement operators19,20,29–32, thereby setting a performance benchmark for past and future detector tomography experiments. In addition to providing the first fundamental bound for detector estimation, the DQFI enables us to draw the following physical insights: 1) We draw a direct analogy between the DQFI and the well-known state quantum Fisher information (SQFI), finding some similarities and some surprising differences. 2) We apply the DQFI to noisy on-off single-photon detectors16,24,25 and implement the first provably-optimal detector estimation experiment using the IBM platform. 3) We show that the proposed DQFI framework provides an alternative approach for optimal sensing of a quantum process18, which requires both optimal probe states and optimal measurements (Fig. 1(c)). In practice, our alternative approach could lead to more appropriate benchmarks in settings where probe preparation capabilities by far exceed control over the measurement device.

Overall, our work reveals surprising connections between the theories of state and detector tomography while highlighting the unique aspects of detector analysis. These findings complete the triad of optimal state, process, and detector tomography (Fig. 1)16,24, paving the way for a more balanced role of states and measurements in precision quantum metrology.

## Results

Introduction to the framework
Before introducing precision bounds for the estimation of quantum measurements, we briefly recap the concept of efficiency and how it leads to precision bounds in quantum state estimation17,29–34. The task here (Fig. 1(a)) is to estimate parameters θ of an unknown state ρ θ, by first measuring the state via a m-outcome POVM, Π ≡ {π 1,…,π m}, and then processing the measured probabilities, p θ (j)=Tr(ρ θ π j ), to get the parameter estimates17. The efficiency or effectiveness of the measurement Π in extracting parameter information depends on how sensitive its measured statistics are to changes in the parameter value. In the local setting, where the unknown parameters are close to some known true values17,30, efficiency is quantified by the classical Fisher information (CFI) of the distribution17,35–37,

F θ [ρ θ,Π] := ∑ j∈[m] (∂ θ p θ (j))2 / p θ (j) = E p θ (∂ θ log p θ )2 , (1)

capturing the variance of the parameter-derivative ∂ θ p θ/p θ of the distribution (abbreviating ∂ θ := ∂/∂ θ and [m]:={1,…,m}). The minimum mean-squared error (MSE) of parameter estimates achievable (on average per trial) using a measurement Π is given by 1/F θ, as per the classical CRB (CCRB)31. Accordingly, optimal measurements are those that maximise the CFI in Eq. (1), thus minimising the CCRB and yielding the most precise estimates17,38,39. However, maximising this non-linear quantity is challenging in practice, even more so in the multi-parameter case38,39, so the state QFI (SQFI) I θ of state ρ θ was introduced as an upper bound to the maximum CFI over all measurements29–31. The SQFI is defined as

I θ [ρ θ]:=Tr(ρ θ L2 θ )=E ρ θ [L2 θ ], and satisfies

max Π F θ [ρ θ,Π] ≤ I θ [ρ θ] (2)

for any valid ρ θ, with equality holding in several cases17,34. The symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) operator L θ appearing in the definition generalises the classical logarithmic derivative ∂ θ log p θ in Eq. (1) implicitly via L θ ρ θ+ρ θ L θ=2∂ θ ρ θ. Following Eq. (2), the QCRB given by 1/I θ lower-bounds the MSE of estimates for any measurement Π, thus setting a precision bound31. In the following, we introduce a general framework for bounding estimation precision for parameters of quantum measurements. To start off, we consider detector models with a single unknown parameter; these are relevant for practical single-photon detectors and noisy qubit detectors. Then, we generalise the framework to multi-parameter scenarios, addressing general quantum detector tomography.

Single-parameter detector estimation
The task here (Fig. 1(b)) is to characterise an unknown m-outcome measurement Π θ ≡ {π jθ } j∈[m] by first probing it with a known quantum state ρ in, and then processing the measured probabilities, p θ (j)=Tr(ρ in π jθ ), to obtain parameter estimates. The efficiency of the probe state ρ in in extracting parameter information from Π θ is determined by the CFI, F θ [ρ in , Π θ], which leads to the CCRB, 1/F θ, lower-bounding MSE when using this probe. Thus, the optimal or most precise probe state, ρopt, is the one maximising the CFI, i.e.,

ρopt[Π θ] := argmax ρ in F θ [ρ in , Π θ], (3)

F θmax [Π θ] := max ρ in F θ [ρ in , Π θ].

The maximisation in Eq. (3) has no known analytical solution, though numerical techniques from channel literature may be applicable40. Specifically, by translating the detector POVM to Kraus operators for quantum-classical maps (particular choice of Kraus set shown in Eq. (27)), the maximisation for F θmax can, in principle, be converted to a maximisation over all equivalent Kraus operators through a numerical semi-definite program40. In practice, however, this approach is computationally demanding due to the large number of Kraus operators for a measurement channel. The question of the optimal probe state is thus a significant hurdle for detector tomography, although it has been addressed for specific measurement channels41,42. The lack of efficiently computable precision bounds for the minimum MSE, 1/F θmax , for detector estimation reveals a gap in our understanding of the information content of measurements and resulting fundamental limits on estimation errors.

We now clarify how the domain of maximisation in Eq. (3) corresponds to various probing strategies for detector estimation. Let H d denote the d-dimensional Hilbert space of probe states and D(H d ) the space of density matrices on H d. The simplest probing strategy is to pick a single state, ρ in , from D(H d ) to probe the detector, repeatedly and independently. Alternatively, one may use an ensemble of p different probe states, ρ k ∈ D(H d ) for k=1,…,p, each with probability q k (∑ k q k=1). Which strategy is ultimately favoured? As we show in Lemma 1 in Methods, from the convexity of the CFI37, a single quantum state is sufficient to be optimal.

Central to the CFI and the SQFI is the logarithmic derivative quantity: both information measures capture the variance of this quantity, as in Eq. (1). To quantify it, we introduce the SLD operators for each measurement operator. For each outcome j ∈ [m] of Π θ, we define an SLD operator L jθ via

L jθ π jθ +π jθ L jθ := 2∂ θ π jθ : (4)

This implicit definition has known solutions in terms of the measurement operators and their parameter derivatives (Eqs. (18), (19) in Methods)43. More importantly, the SLD operators let us express the measurement probabilities p θ (j|ρ)=Tr(ρπ jθ ) and their derivatives ∂ θ p θ (j|ρ)=Tr(ρ∂ θ π jθ )=Re Tr(π jθ ρL jθ ) as linear operations on the state and the measurement (where Re[⋅] denotes real part)17,34. These two expressions, when substituted into the CFI in Eq. (1), open the door to operator inequalities that can gauge F θmax without actual optimisation17.

DQFI definition
To upper-bound F θ by an expression independent of ρ, we borrow from state estimation a chain of inequalities17,34 that, when applied to the CFI expressed in terms of π jθ , L jθ , and ρ, yields

F θ [ρ, Π θ] ≤ ∑ j∈[m] |Tr(√π jθ ρ L jθ )|2 / Tr(ρπ jθ ) ≤ Tr(Q θ ρ), (5)

where Q θ := ∑ j∈[m] L jθ π jθ L jθ is a positive semi-definite operator. The first inequality above relies on Re[z]2 ≤ |z|2 for complex number z, whereas the second is the operator Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. In state estimation we obtain the measurement-independent SQFI I θ at this point, but here the trace quantity upper-bounding F θ still depends on ρ. Our final step settles this by maximising both sides of Eq. (5) over the probe space D(H d ), resulting in F θmax ≤ max ρ∈D(H d) Tr(Q θ ρ)= ||Q θ ||2 sp , where ||⋅||2 sp denotes the largest eigenvalue (or spectral radius) of Q θ. Moreover, the probe state maximising Tr(Q θ ρ) is the eigenvector of Q θ corresponding to its largest eigenvalue—this state is thus always pure.

These results lay the ground for defining the DQFI: an upper bound to the maximum CFI that leads to precision bounds for detector estimation. We propose two definitions for the DQFI.

Definition 1. (Spectral DQFI). Define the spectral DQFI J jj,θ of a measurement Π θ ≡ {π jθ } j∈[m] as

J jj,θ [Π θ] := || ∑ j∈[m] L jθ π jθ L jθ ||2 sp , (6)

where ||X||2 sp denotes the spectral radius or largest eigenvalue of operator X.

A simpler but less tight upper bound on F θmax worth consideration is Tr Q θ. In fact, Tr Q θ= ∑ j∈[m] Tr(π jθ L j 2 θ ) resembles the SQFI I θ. Assembling the measurement operators and their SLD counterparts into md × md block-diagonal operators Π θ,bd := ⊕ j∈[m] π jθ and L θ,bd := ⊕ j∈[m] L jθ reveals Tr Q θ=Tr(Π θ,bd L2 θ,bd )=I θ (Π θ,bd ). This approach is justified in that Π θ,bd is trace-constant (though not unit-trace) like a state and L θ,bd is indeed its SLD operator when treated as such. This weaker upper bound results from treating the measurement as an unnormalised, higher-dimensional state.

Definition 2. (Trace DQFI). Define the trace DQFI J Tr,θ of a measurement Π θ ≡ {π jθ } j∈[m] as

J Tr,θ [Π θ]:= ∑ j∈[m] Tr(L jθ π jθ L jθ ). (7)

Having proposed two definitions for the DQFI, we must compare the two to understand their maximum disagreement and cases where they are equivalent. It is evident from the positivity of Q θ that J jj,θ ≤ J Tr,θ. On the other hand, the largest eigenvalue of Q θ cannot be smaller than the average of its eigenvalues, so that J Tr,θ ≤ d J jj,θ. This leads to the following ordering of the DQFIs,

1/d J Tr,θ ≤ J jj,θ ≤ J Tr,θ ≤ d J jj,θ : (8)

The cause of the disagreement clarifies why the spectral DQFI is tighter—it respects that quantum states are normalised, so that probing along multiple directions requires sacrificing some probability of detection, and hence parameter information, along each direction. Nonetheless, the trace DQFI serves as a simpler upper bound that is more amenable to analytical evaluation.

To consolidate the two DQFI definitions, we propose Theorem 1 in the following.

Theorem 1. (DQFI upper-bounds maximum CFI). For estimating quantum detectors, the spectral DQFI J jj,θ and the trace DQFI J Tr,θ upper-bound the maximum CFI over probe states, F θmax , as F θmax ≤ J jj,θ ≤ J Tr,θ.

Proof. The proof follows from Eqs. (5) and (8) and is provided in Methods.

Theorem 1 leads to the trace QCRB 1/J Tr,θ and the spectral QCRB 1/J jj,θ, which lower-bound the minimum MSE of estimates as 1/J Tr,θ ≤ 1/J jj,θ ≤ 1/F θmax , thereby setting precision bounds for detector estimation.

Example 1. We now present a simple example to illustrate the importance of the DQFI. Consider a qubit Z-basis detector with inherent bit-flip noise4 of unknown strength p (0 ≤ p ≤ 1), corresponding to the POVM Π p ≡ {π 1p ,π 2p } with

π 1p = (1-p 0; 0 p), π 2p = (p 0; 0 1-p). (9)

Figure 2(a) illustrates the Fisher information in estimating p for both non-optimal and optimal probe states. We find that the spectral DQFI (dashed black curve) is tight, as it equals the maximum CFI F θmax . The Fisher information for probe states notated as |θ,ϕ⟩ := cos(θ/2)|0⟩+exp(iϕ)sin(θ/2)|1⟩ is depicted as circular markers (orange, purple and blue) on dashed lines for non-optimal probes, and as star-shaped markers (golden) for the optimal probes. The DQFI J jj,p is 4/(1/〈Z〉2-(1-2p)2) where 〈Z〉=Tr(ρZ) is the Pauli Z expectation of ρ. The CFI is maximised at 〈Z〉=±1, corresponding to |0⟩ or |1⟩, attaining a maximum of F pmax =1/p(1-p) in either case (golden points). As Q p=1/p(1-p) 1 2, its eigenstates are also |0⟩ and |1⟩. Thus, the maximum CFI over probe states equals J jj,p and is attained by probes |0⟩ or |1⟩, in agreement with J jj,p. Here we have J Tr,p=2F pmax =2J jj,p, displaying the maximum disagreement possible for d=2.

Attainability of DQFI
In the above example, the spectral DQFI is attainable, i.e., J jj,θ=F θmax , and the optimal probe states are among the basis states. These two statements are generally true for diagonal or phase-insensitive measurements, because inequality (5) is saturated, as we state in the following theorem.

Theorem 2. (Attainability for diagonal measurements). For estimating a phase-insensitive detector represented by a diagonal POVM Π θ, the DQFI J jj,θ is attainable, i.e., J jj,θ = F θmax , and an optimal probe exists within the family of basis states.

Proof. The proof is presented in Supplementary Mat. I.

Phase-insensitive measurements feature prominently in detector characterisation experiments, in part because they do not require phase stabilisation of probes16,24. Indeed, avalanche photodiodes (APDs)16,24, multiplexed photon-number-resolving detectors16,24,25, and superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors26,27,44 have been experimentally characterised in this setting. Given the extensive usage of these detectors across quantum technologies, understanding the information-theoretic bounds for estimating them has practical implications for benchmarking existing approaches to detector characterisation and designing more effective strategies. Our result in Theorem 2 means that the spectral QCRB sets the ultimate precision limit here.

The proof of Theorem 2 also covers measurements that are simultaneously diagonalisable independent of the parameters (see Supplementary Mat. I). This category includes qubit detectors with phase-flip noise (Fig. 2(b)) and bit-phase-flip noise (Fig. 2(c))4, so the spectral DQFI is tight for all single-Pauli error qubit detectors. More generally, we find a necessary condition for attainability of the spectral DQFI to be that the SLD operators commute, [L jθ , L kθ ]=0, akin to compatible multi-parameter state estimation14,17,36,45,46 (see Theorem 3 in Methods for the complete set of necessary and sufficient attainability criteria). However, if the SLD operators do not commute, the spectral DQFI could be unattainable even in the single-parameter regime, which is not the case in state estimation. Interestingly, in this case, the attainable bound can be computed through a semi-definite program (Supplementary Mat. II) that effectively incorporates non-Hermitian components into the SLD operator definition in Eq. (4) (see Methods).

Platform demonstration
We now consider a simple, but practically relevant and experimentally feasible example, of estimating a qubit detector affected by dephasing noise4. Given that dephasing is particularly prominent on current quantum computing platforms47,48, its precise characterisation is crucial for effective noise control and suppression. Other noise models4 are deferred to Supplementary Mat. III.

Example 2. Consider a generic dephased qubit projective measurement, corresponding to the POVM Π p ≡ {π 1p ,π 2p } with elements

π 1p = 1/2 (1 + (1-2p)cosθ sinθ e-iϕ; (1-2p)sinθ eiϕ 1-cosθ), π 2p = 1/2 (1 - (1-2p)cosθ sinθ e-iϕ; -(1-2p)sinθ eiϕ 1+cosθ), (10)

where p denotes the unknown dephasing strength (0 ≤ p ≤ 1/2). Here, the noiseless measurement Π ideal corresponding to p=0 is assumed known. It corresponds to projections along polar and azimuthal angles θ and ϕ on the Bloch sphere (double arrows in Fig. 3(b)), via two orthogonal projectors, |± θ,ϕ⟩, given by the nontrivial eigenvectors of π 1p |p=0. The spectral and trace DQFI can be calculated as

J k,p = sin2θ / p(1-p) & J Tr,p = 2sin2θ / p(1-p) : (11)

The two optimal probe states, ρ± opt, are both pure and have phase ϕ, thus lying in the same vertical plane as measurement projectors |± θ,ϕ⟩, as shown in Fig. 3(a). This observation, magnified in Fig. 3(b), provides an intuitive explanation of the optimal probes (black dots in Fig. 3(b)): they are the pure states that align perfectly with the measurement direction upon dephasing. The polar angles θ ± opt of these optimal probes, given by tanθ ± opt = ±tanθ/(1-2p), can be deduced geometrically from Fig. 3(b).

We now experimentally implement Example 2 on an IBM Eagle r3 quantum computer as follows. First, we introduce dephasing noise of fixed strength p=0.2 by interacting the probe qubit with an ancilla qubit (Fig. 3(c)). Then we estimate the noise strength using a range of probe states, including both optimal and non-optimal ones (see Methods for details). Critically, the noiseless measurement is fixed at (θ, ϕ) = (π/8, 0), differentiating the problem from state or process estimation. In Fig. 3(d), we compare the experimental MSEs for each probe state (blue dots) to the CCRB 1/F p (black curve) that gives the theoretical minimum MSE20 for this probe state and to the MSEs from noiseless simulation (green dots). The spectral QCRB 1/J k,p (horizontal blue dashed line) lower-bounds the MSE for any probe state. The theory-optimal (vertical black dashed line), simulated-optimal and experimentally-inferred optimal probes agree within confidence intervals (green and blue regions), consistent with platform noise.

In contrast to previous efforts to characterise the platform’s SPAM errors through detector tomography22, which do not use optimal quantum states, our work provides the first instance of provably optimal detector tomography.

Multi-parameter detector tomography
In quantum state estimation, there are many physically motivated scenarios where we will want to estimate multiple parameters simultaneously13,14,49–54. Similarly, the example is full detector tomography, where the maximal number of unknown parameters is simultaneously inferred (see below and Refs. 16, 24 for more examples). For state estimation, it is known that measuring the parameters simultaneously can provide greater sensitivity compared to measuring them sequentially55. Analogously, multiple parameters of a detector can be successively estimated using the single-parameter framework56, but achieving the ultimate precision limit requires the simultaneous estimation of all parameters. In this setting, the CFI is a matrix reflecting the probe’s sensitivity to each parameter individually as well as correlations in sensitivities to multiple parameters (defined in Eq. (SM.VII.1), Supplementary Mat. VII). The corresponding QCRBs minimise a weighted-sum of the different parameter variances and covariances18, but an ensemble of probe states is generally required (see discussion in Methods). For simplicity, here, we set the weight to identity and minimise total MSE of the parameters, though our techniques also apply to arbitrary weight matrices (see Supplementary Mat. VII). Below, we propose two QCRBs that lower-bound the attainable minimum total MSE, which is defined as the minimum CCRB over all probing ensembles,

CCCRB := min Tr(F θ -1) : (12)

We first extend the trace DQFI to the multi-parameter setting. For estimating n real parameters, θ:=(θ 1,…,θ n), the trace DQFI from Def. 2 symmetrically extends to the n×n real matrix J Tr,θ with elements

(J Tr,θ ) jk := 1/2 ∑ l∈[m] Tr(L l θ j π l L l θ k +L l θ k π l L l θ j ), (13)

where L l θ j is the SLD operator for the lth outcome and the jth parameter. This matrix upper-bounds the CFI matrix for any probing strategy as J Tr,θ ≽ F θ (Theorem 5 in Supplementary Mat. VII), where A ≽ 0 denotes A is positive semi-definite. The trace QCRB, CQCRB Tr := Tr J Tr,θ -1, thus lower-bounds CCCRB in Eq. (12). However, due to the limitation discussed below Eq. (8), the trace QCRB is generally unattainable, as in Example 3.

Next we consider the more complex problem of extending the spectral DQFI to the spectral QCRB, denoted CQCRB k. This is done through an efficient semi-definite program (in Supplementary Mat. VII), where we define a linear objective that is maximised, symmetrically extending Tr(Q θ ρ) from Eq. (5) to multiple parameters. This results in a bound tighter than the trace QCRB, see Supplementary Mat. VII for details. Notably, the spectral QCRB does not require considering an ensemble of probes, unlike the minimisation in Eq. (12), thus offering a practical computational advantage.

Example 3 below compares the two QCRBs to CCCRB, showing the spectral bound to be tight for an experimentally relevant problem16,24,25.

Example 3. Consider the tomography of a phase-insensitive, on-off qubit detector. The POVM Π θ ≡ {π 1θ ,π 2θ } representing such a measurement may be parametrised as

π 1θ = (θ/2 0; 0 1-θ/2), π 2θ = (1-θ/2 0; 0 θ/2). (14)

The trace DQFI for simultaneously estimating θ≡{θ 1,θ 2} is

J Tr,θ = diag(θ 1(1-θ 1), θ 2(1-θ 2)),

and the resulting QCRB is CQCRB Tr = ∑ j=1 2 1/θ j(1-θ j). The spectral QCRB for this problem is

CQCRB k = (∑ j=1 2 1/√(θ j(1-θ j)))2 = Tr J Tr,θ -1 = CQCRB Tr + 2/θ(1-θ)θ 2(1-θ 2).

The spectral QCRB is attainable, i.e., CCCRB=CQCRB k. The optimal probing strategy requires an ensemble of two states: |0⟩ and |1⟩ prepared with probability q and 1-q in the proportion q/(1-q) = √(θ 1(1-θ 1))/√(θ 2(1-θ 2)).

Probeincompatibility effect
An interesting feature of Example 3 is that the optimal multi-parameter probing strategy is a convex mixture of the single-parameter optimal probes, namely, |0⟩ and |1⟩ for θ 1 and θ 2, respectively. Although this may not hold for generic multi-parameter models, it underscores the fact that when the optimal single-parameter probes for different parameters are incompatible, termed probe incompatibility in Ref. 56, there is an uncertainty trade-off in simultaneous multi-parameter estimation. Naturally, we can expect the optimal simultaneous strategy to generally outperform the optimal strategy that utilizes a fraction of detector uses to estimate each parameter separately. This latter strategy, which we call sequential multi-parameter estimation, is connected to the total QFI metric56, and we compare our bounds to this metric in Supplementary Mat. VIII. While the comparison shows the spectral technique to produce a tighter bound than the total QFI metric56, the former approach may still be viewed as a special case of a particular choice of channel purification and computation of the corresponding QFI matrix.

Application to photodetector tomography
Example 3 generalises to phase-insensitive measurements of higher-dimensional states, such as the APDs experimentally tomographed in Refs. 16, 24, 25. These detectors correspond to diagonal two-outcome measurements in the photon number basis for the continuous-variable state space, truncated at some large dimension d. The spectral QCRB here, CQCRB k = (∑ j=1 d 1/√(θ j(1-θ j)))2, is tight and sets the precision limit for APD tomography. Attaining this precision requires preparing an ensemble of photon-number states {|j⟩}, each with probability q j ∝ √(θ j(1-θ j)), and assigning a higher q j to states |j⟩ that produce more uniformly distributed detection probabilities. Interestingly, the spectral QCRB in Eq. (15) mirrors the Gill-Massar QCRB for state estimation57, with similar behaviour seen in Fig. 2(d) for the simultaneous estimation of bit-flip and phase-flip rates (Example 4 in Supplementary Mat. VII).

## Methods

Probing strategies for detector estimation
Local unbiased estimation. In the local estimation setting, where unknown parameters θ are close to known true values θ*, the Fisher information framework requires locally-unbiased estimators, meaning estimators with zero bias at the true parameter values17,35,70. Effectively, this constrains how the probabilistic detector outcomes are mapped to corresponding predicted values for the unknown parameters20. In linear estimation20,28, this is done through a classical estimator function represented by an m×n real matrix Ξ jk that, given a detector outcome j∈[m], predicts the estimate Ξ jk for θ k(k∈[n]). The overall estimate produced for each θ k is then ∑ j p θ (j)Ξ jk. The local-unbiasedness condition is then ∑ j p θ (j)Ξ jk |θ=θ*=θ k. The maximum-likelihood estimator is asymptotically unbiased, and therefore can saturate the CCRB in that limit20.

Single-parameter detector estimation. We first present Lemma 1, establishing single-probe strategies to be sufficient for optimal single-parameter detector estimation.

Lemma 1. For single-parameter detector estimation, a single-probe strategy is optimal and at least one optimal state ρopt ∈ D(H d ) exists that attains F θmax in Eq. (3).

Proof of Lemma 1. Suppose, to estimate a single parameter θ of a measurement Π θ, we probe with two distinct states, ρ 1 ≠ ρ 2, ρ 1, ρ 2 ∈ D(H d ), with probabilities q 1 and q 2 = 1-q 1. The joint list of probabilities,

plist={q 1 p θ (1|ρ 1), ..., q 1 p θ (m|ρ 1), q 2 p θ (1|ρ 2), ..., q 2 p θ (m|ρ 2)},

forms a valid distribution and, as q j are (by definition) independent of θ, we see from Eq. (1) that the CFI of plist,

F θ [plist]=q 1 F θ [ρ 1, Π θ]+(1-q 1)F θ [ρ 2, Π θ], (16)

is a convex combination of the CFIs of each probe ρ k individually. Unless the two individual CFIs are equal, the combined CFI F θ [plist] is smaller than the maximum individual CFI. Even if the two individual CFIs are equal, combining them with the only probe ρ 1 or only ρ 2 is sufficient for proving optimality. Thus, for single-parameter detector estimation, a one-state probing strategy is optimal.

Lemma 1 says that for single parameters, the maximisation in Eq. (3) can be performed over ρ in ∈ D(H d ).

Multi-parameter detector estimation. For multi-parameter problems, Lemma 1 does not hold and an ensemble of probes is generally required for optimality. This is because multiple unknown parameters cannot be uniquely determined without sufficiently many linearly-independent outcome probabilities. The multi-parameter CFI matrix F θ for an ensemble {q k, ρ k} k∈[p] comprising p probe states is a convex sum of the individual CFI matrices F θ [ρ k, Π θ] = ∑ k q k F θ [ρ k, Π θ], (17)

similar to Eq. (16). Here, the difference from the single-parameter setting is that the CCRB Tr(F θ -1) requires matrix inversion of F θ. We note that even if the individual CFI matrices are equal, the combined CFI matrix F θ [ρ k, Π θ] = F θ [ρ k, Π θ] is not necessarily equal to the individual matrices, and the inverse of the sum is not the sum of the inverses. In general, the minimum number of probes required for estimating n parameters is ⌈n/(m-1)⌉, where m is the number of outcomes. For n parameters, the optimal strategy is an ensemble of probes {q k, ρ k} k∈[p] that can be used to estimate each parameter simultaneously. However, this minimum number of probes merely guarantees the feasibility of multi-parameter estimation, whereas optimality may require even larger ensembles.

Notably, an ensemble of p different d-dimensional probe states can be realised through access to an ancillary system, A, that can be measured perfectly. This involves preparing a single bipartite-entangled state in D(H d ⊗ HA p ), where HA p denotes the p-dimensional Hilbert space corresponding to system A. For example, the ensemble {q k, ρ k} can be realised by preparing the state ∑ k √q k |ρ k⟩ ⊗ |k⟩A and measuring the ancilla perfectly in the {|k⟩A} basis28. In this sense, Lemma 1 extends to multi-parameter problems, with the optimisation domain becoming ρ in ∈ D(H d ⊗ HA p ).

The equivalence between bipartite-entangled states and ensemble probes means that unless the probe and ancilla are measured jointly, the convexity of the CFI (Lemma 1) rules out any entanglement advantage in precision in the single-parameter setting. However, for the most general estimation scenario, ancilla measurements conditioned on the detector outcomes should be considered. This estimation strategy was applied to detector tomography in Ref. 28 and extended to imperfect but pre-characterised ancilla measurements. In Supplementary Mat. II, using Theorem 4, we show that for single-parameter detector estimation, even conditional measurements cannot enable an entanglement advantage, and the maximum precision can be attained using a single separable pure-state probe. At the same time, the advantages of ancilla-assisted probe states for multi-parameter detector estimation have been addressed in recent experimental demonstrations71,72, though the extent of precision enhancement remains to be explored.

Single-parameter DQFI derivation
The Lyapunov equation (4) can be explicitly solved by utilising either the eigenspectrum of π jθ = ∑ k∈[d] λ jk |λ jk⟩⟨λ jk|17,29,30,
