### Reviewer 1

This paper introduces new tools to determine the ultimate precision limits of quantum detectors. Detector characterization involves determining the associated POVMs, a task addressed by quantum detector tomography (QDT). In QDT, an unknown element \Pi_k is characterized through a set of known measurements using known input probe states. By performing many repetitions on multiple copies of each probe state, one can estimate \Pi_k, thereby allowing the inverse problem to be solved.
Following the pioneering work of Ian Walmsley's group, QDT has been performed for a wide range of detectors, including SPADs, time-multiplexed detectors, transition-edge sensors, superconducting nanowire detectors, and even the human eye. Due to the complexity of the task, various advanced methods have been developed, such as the Fitting of Data Patterns, self-guided tomography, compressed sensing tomography, and techniques based on neural networks. To the best of my knowledge, all of these approaches rely on fidelity (or variants thereof) for benchmarking.
The current work introduces a novel tool: the detector quantum Fisher information (DQFI). The concept is elegant and the theoretical development is clear. The authors propose two definitions of DQFI—one tighter than the other. While this is insightful, I would appreciate a clearer operational preference or justification for using one over the other.
The authors draw an analogy with the standard quantum Fisher information (QFI). But we know that for pure states, QFI reduces to the variance of the generator. In this sense, QFI provides a lower bound on the mean square error (MSE), which can be related to fidelity. From a benchmarking standpoint, I question whether this represents a significant advance over existing approaches in QDT.
More importantly, it is well known that a key requirement for QDT is that the set of probe states must be experimentally feasible. This means the states must be well-characterized themselves. In standard tomography once the QFI is known and the quantum Cramér-Rao bound (QCRB) is shown to be saturable, one can advantageously identify the optimal probe states for characterization. The authors focus on the single-parameter case, where the situation is relatively simple. Can this be done for QDT?
However, a complete QDT requires a multiparameter scenario, where the QCRB is generally not saturable. In standard QDT, the set of reference states must be tomographically complete; i.e., they must span the space of POVMs to enable inversion. In photodetector measurements, this is relatively straightforward. Coherent states of an optical beam serve as ideal candidates: they are overcomplete and can form a tomographically complete set by varying amplitude (e.g., via attenuation with a beam splitter) and phase (e.g., with a delay line). Crucially, such states are easy to generate using lasers.
A question that remains is whether the proposed DQFI can be used to identify optimal probe states for full QDT. In the standard multiparameter QFI framework, one can convert the QCRB matrix into a scalar bound (e.g., via a trace with a weighting matrix) and thereby derive optimal states. Would a similar approach be possible or meaningful in the DQFI context?
In summary, this is a well-written and rigorous work introducing new concepts that may prove important in refining the limits of QDT. I recommend it for publication. However, I believe that addressing the concerns mentioned above would enhance the readability and practical impact of the paper.

### Reviewer 2

The authors investigate the precision achievable in estimation of parameters of general quantum measurements. The authors introduce detector quantum Fisher information, investigate its properties and present applications of the established formalism. The present study is comprehensive and it nicely complements the earlier results established of optimal estimation of parameters encoded in quantum states. As pointed out by the authors in the Supplemental material, there are close connections between quantum measurements and quantum processes. The quantum measurement can be seen as a specific instance of a quantum process (or quantum channel), where the output state is one of orthogonal states associated with the measurement outcomes, c.f. Eq. (SM8.3) when traced over the second degree of freedom. Nevertheless, the quantum measurements play so important role that it is fully justified to treat them separately and establish a theory which provides bounds on precision of estimation of parameters encoded in the measurements. Given the central role that sophisticated quantum measurements play in modern quantum technologies and quantum computing architectures the potential impact and importance of the present work are high enough to in principle deserve publication in Nature Communications.
There are several points that should be considered by the authors before the manuscript could be published:
1) In the Supplemental Material 7 the authors consider a scenario where two copies of the measurement are available. In this case, entangled probe states may be optimal and may provide advantage. What about using entangled probes when probing a single copy of the measurement. Suppose a pure bipartite entangled states of systems A and B is prepared and the measurement is applied to system A. Subsequently, also system B is measured and the measurement on B can depend on the outcome of the measurement performed on system A. Could such scenario provide any advantage with respect to using only a single system A to probe the characterized quantum measurement? Note that the entanglement of A and B need not be maximal.
2) The authors base their work on the widely utilized concept of Fisher information. To saturate the Cramer-Rao bound, an unbiased estimator is usually required. The authors should clarify in more details which estimators do they have in mind in general, whether they assume the maximum likelihood estimator in the asymptotic limit of very large number of samples.
3) In the Supplemental Material 3, the authors provide an example of a linear estimator of parameter p, Eq. (SM.3.2). What are the signs of the coefficients alpha and beta in this estimator? It seems that one of the coefficients is negative. In principle, the estimator can yield a negative value of the estimated parameter, which would be unphysical. This may happen in case of low number of samples and if the true p is close to 0. While such situations may be rare in occurrence, the authors should comment on this, because e.g. changing the negative p to p=0 could introduce a bias in the estimator.
4) The authors should check Eq. (SM.8.16).
5) In Figure 1 in the Supplemental Material, symbol theta denotes both the angle of a probe quantum state and also the unknown parameter to be estimated. The authors should check the notation used in this figure.

### Reviewer 3

The authors of the paper, propose the concept of detector quantum fisher information (DQFI), which in their words, feels the gap in the triad “State, Process and Measurements”. They claim that while State and Process estimation are well investigated fields, the Measurement estimation problem is not. They derive the upper bound on the achievable classical information in terms of DQFI, which they show to be saturable for a subclass of diagonal povms. They propose also a generalization to multi-parameter case, and discuss an experimental using the IBM quantum computing platform.
The paper is in my opinion correct, and also highlights in an interesting way the relevance of measurement estimation problem. There is a serious issue with the paper, however, which authors are either not aware or intentionally avoid discussion of.
Any quantum measurement is a special case of a quantum channel, more concretely a quantum-classical channel! Given any generalized measurement, with measurement operators \pi_j, I can construct a corresponding channel with Kraus operators K_j = |j> \sqrt{\pi_j}, where outputs represent measurement outcomes.
I can now use all the results from quantum channel estimation theory to obtain channel QFI – which in this case will correspond to DQFI. In particular, in J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. , 41 p. 255304 (2008) , it is shown that channel QFI is upper bounded by 4 | \sum_i \dot{K}_i^\dagger \dot{K}_i|, where the norm is the spectral norm, and \dot{K}_i are derivatives of Kraus operators. In our case since, we can plug in operators K_j = |j> \sqrt{\pi_j}, and use identity \dot{(K_i^\dagger K_i)} = \dot{K_i}^\dagger K_i + K_i^\dagger \dot{K_i}. to effectively get the result (6) obtained by the authors.
Moreover, the above result from quantum channel estimation theory is much stronger than the result presented by the authors, as one can prove its general saturability provided one minimizes the channel over different Kraus representations. Furthermore, this problem may be implemented as a simple SDP programme as was shown in Nat. Commun. , Vol. 3 p. 1063 (2012). Hence, these tools are much more powerful than the ones proposed by the authors.
Regarding the multi-parameter case, it should be stressed here, that the non-trivial issue here is the ‘probe-incomplatibilty’ , which has been also investigated thoroughly in the quantum channel estimation literature, see e.g. Phys. Rev. X , Vol. 12 p. 011039 (2022). In particular in this reference, a generalization of Fujiwara bound to multiparameter case is given. I presume that this bound again would allow for a more efficient numerical analysis than the bound proposed by the authors, as it again may be solved using the SPD. This at least should at least be tested and compared.
In the light of these results, the novely of the presented work is not as high as might seem at a first sight. Still, despite this harsh criticism, I would not formulae here a negative recommendation yet. Provided the Authors are able to show that they are able to propose an improved tools compared to the ones I mentioned above, making use of the particular structure of the quantum-claasical channel that represents the measurement process and showing that they are superior to the all-purpose channel estimation methods.
In particular, if authors were able to show that minimization over different Kraus representations, that is required to find the channel QFI in the general case, can be simplified for the detector QFI case – ideally solved analytically!- and show some insight behind it I would regard this as an important contribution to the field. In the same spirit If the authors show that their multi-parameter approach is superior to existing channel estimation approaches, this would be an argument in favour of this paper to be published in Nat Comm. Otherwise, the paper may at most be regarded as a nice highlight of an important special case of a problem which has a known solution, and as such does not meet the standards of Nat. Comm.
Apart from this main criticism, I have some minor remarks:
- Above Eq.(2) the authors write: “. However, this maximisation is not tractable in general [38, 39],” This is only true for multi-parameter case. For single parameter this problem is completely solved, and hence this sentence will be misleading for the readers, as immediately below the authors present single parameter formulas
- Authors do not mention the possibility of using an ancilla with which the probe state is entangled. I guess in this case this would not help, as the quantum channel we consider is quantum-classical, but It would be nice at least to comment this.
- Below Eq.3 Authors write “The maximization is not analytically tractable”. This is true, but in the light of what I wrote, above it is also slightly misleading, as there are efficient methods to find channel QFI with a simple SDP programme.
